h1: Scalp Folliculitis: Why Those Bumps Hurt and What Clears Them
subtitle: Tender, sometimes pus-filled bumps sitting right on the follicle.

hero.alt: 200x close-up of the scalp showing small red bumps centered on the follicle openings with yellow crusting, with hairs still emerging
hero.caption: Red bumps centered on the follicle openings, with hairs still coming through. At 200x.

quickAnswer: Scalp folliculitis is inflammation of the hair follicle itself. It shows up as small tender bumps, sometimes with a white head, usually with a hair coming through the center. It can sting, itch or feel sore to the touch, and it often clusters at the back of the head, along the hairline, or wherever a style sits tight. Most cases involve bacteria, yeast or occlusion from product buildup, sweat and covered hair. It is not a hygiene failure. Left running for months, repeated inflammation around the same follicles can cost you hair, which is why persistent bumps deserve a proper look. We read your scalp at 200x at Nina Ross Atlanta in Sandy Springs. Serving all of Metro Atlanta.
takeaways: It is inflammation of the follicle itself.
It is not a hygiene failure.
Bacterial and yeast types need different care.

items.you: Sore bumps with a hair in the middle
items.why: A tender bump centered on a hair is the classic sign of folliculitis, commonly linked to bacteria, yeast or buildup at the follicle opening.
items.check: We read the bumps at 200x to see whether they look bacterial or yeast-driven, because each needs different care.

items.why: Stinging when you brush is commonly linked to inflamed follicles reacting to touch and tension.
items.check: We read the tender areas at 200x and look at what your styling and products are putting on the scalp.

items.you: They keep coming back in the same spots
items.why: Bumps that return in the same spots are commonly linked to a cause that has not been addressed, often the wrong type being treated.
items.check: We identify the type first, then re-check the same area at follow-up instead of assuming it cleared.

items.why: Crusting is what a pustule leaves after it breaks. Picking or popping can spread irritation to nearby follicles.
items.check: We read the crusted areas and the skin around them to see how far the inflammation reaches.

items.you: Firm bumps at my nape that will not go
items.us: Keloidal papules at the occipital hairline
items.why: Firm bumps at the nape are commonly linked to repeated irritation along the back hairline, especially with fades and close cuts.
items.check: We read the nape at 200x and look at ingrown hairs, friction and cut style, so care fits what is actually there.

items.title: Bacterial or yeast overgrowth
items.text: Staph species and Malassezia yeast are both common. They behave differently and respond to different care, which is why guessing is expensive.

items.title: Occlusion and buildup
items.text: Heavy product, sweat under a style, and a scalp that stays covered create the warm, occluded environment the follicle reacts to.

items.title: Friction and tension
items.text: Tight styles, helmets and repeated friction irritate the follicle opening and make recurrence more likely.

items.title: Ingrown hairs
items.text: Curved hair re-entering the skin sets off the same inflammatory response, especially at the nape and along faded edges.

insight.text: Treating one as the other is the most common reason scalp bumps keep coming back, which is why we look before we act.

care.title: What care looks like here
care.text: We look at the bumps at 200x to see what we are dealing with, since bacterial and yeast-driven folliculitis look different at the follicle. Care usually starts with deep scalp cleansing to clear buildup, light-based therapy to settle inflammation, and a routine that fits your actual styling life. Then we re-check the same area rather than assuming it cleared.

treatments.text: Low level light used to calm scalp inflammation and support the growth phase.

welcome.title: We are well-versed in us.
paras: Bumps at the nape and hairline are extremely common with textured hair and fades, and they are too often written off as razor bumps or poor hygiene. Neither is a diagnosis. We look at the follicle and treat what is there.
Relaxers, braids, locs, weaves and heat. Share your full hair history. It is welcomed, never judged.

faq.q: Is folliculitis caused by not washing enough?
faq.a: No. Buildup plays a role, and so do bacteria, yeast, friction and ingrown hairs. Plenty of people with meticulous routines get it.

faq.q: Can folliculitis cause permanent hair loss?
faq.a: Left running for months, repeated inflammation around the same follicles can cost you hair. That is why persistent bumps deserve a proper look early.
It is better not to. Popping can spread irritation to nearby follicles and leave marks, especially on deeper skin tones.

faq.q: Why does it come back after antibiotics?
faq.a: One common reason is that the bumps were yeast-driven rather than bacterial, or the buildup and friction behind them never changed. Identifying the type is the first step.

faq.q: Can I keep my braids in?
faq.a: Often, yes. We look at where the bumps are and how tight the style sits, then work out what fits your styling life while the scalp settles.
